content:
### Same Old Apocalypse

By the dragon’s third pass over the city, the clock tower was on fire, three emergency sirens were playing three different songs, and June had decided they were all in a rut.

“Honestly,” she said, dangling by one hand from the minute hand, “I think things have gotten boring.”

Ben tightened his grip on the rope around her waist. “You’re hanging two hundred feet above a burning city.”

“Exactly. Again.”

Below them, the dragon wheeled over the rooftops. It was an impressive creature: scales like black armor, wings broad enough to shadow a bakery, and a royal decree still sticking out of one nostril.

Its name was Vethrak the Inevitable, which June felt was overselling things. So far, it had been extremely evitable.

On the ledge above, Sana loaded a bolt into her crossbow. “What about bowling?”

June considered this as the minute hand gave an alarming creak.

“Isn’t bowling just a dungeon with rental shoes?”

“You don’t get attacked in bowling.”

“You haven’t seen Ben bowl.”

Ben looked wounded. “That was one time.”

“The man behind us lost a tooth.”

“He got it back.”

The dragon landed on the tower roof. Tiles scattered into the street. Its tail smashed the ornamental sundial, which seemed spiteful, as it was after sunset.

“MORTALS,” it thundered. “THE AGE OF—”

“One second,” said Sana.

Vethrak stopped.

June continued, “I just miss doing things we’re bad at. Everything’s become so predictable. Find an ancient relic, ignore the warning, Ben says don’t touch it, Sana touches it—”

“You touched the last one.”

“Because you touched the one before.”

“—and then there’s a chase, a prophecy, somebody loses a shoe, and we save the world before dinner.”

“My left boot is still in the astral plane,” Ben said.

“See? You know what I mean.”

Vethrak lowered its enormous head until one golden eye filled the gap in the clock face.

“I HAVE BURNED NINE KINGDOMS.”

Sana nodded sympathetically. “And did you try varying your routine?”

The dragon blinked.

June’s fingers slipped. Ben hauled on the rope, swore, and hauled again.

“I’m not saying we need less excitement,” June said, swinging over the drop. “I’m saying we used to have dinner together without somebody bleeding on the bread.”

“That happened once,” said Ben.

“It happened twice.”

“The second time was jam.”

“It was arterial.”

Vethrak drew in a long breath. The furnace glow kindled behind its teeth.

Sana raised her crossbow. “Cooking class?”

“We tried that,” June said. “The broth achieved sentience.”

“Pottery?”

“Pottery could work.”

“MORTALS,” Vethrak roared, fire spilling between its fangs, “I AM SPEAKING.”

“So are we,” June snapped.

The dragon recoiled slightly.

Ben took advantage of its surprise and whistled. Sana fired. June let go.

What happened next was technically very impressive.

There was a twang, a clang, and a noise like a piano falling down a spiral staircase. The minute hand snapped upright. June shot past Ben in a blur of rope and swearing. The tower bell tore free of its mounting. Vethrak swallowed its own fire with a deep, disappointed boom.

When the dust settled, June was lying safely on the roof, Ben was sitting in a rain gutter, and Vethrak was in the city fountain with the great bell around its neck.

The bell rang mournfully whenever the dragon moved.

Sana peered over the ledge. “See? Even that was basically the lich in October.”

“It was not,” Ben said.

“You had the same expression.”

“I was concussed in October.”

June sat up and brushed gravel off her sleeves. “Thursday, then. Pottery.”

“Thursday’s the lunar wolves,” said Sana.

“Cancel them.”

“They’re lunar wolves, June. They don’t take cancellations.”

Vethrak thrashed in the fountain. The bell tolled again.

“I HAD A MONOLOGUE,” it said, muffled.

All three friends leaned over the roof.

June cupped her hands around her mouth. “We’re sorry!”

“SIX WEEKS,” the dragon howled. “I WORKED ON IT FOR SIX WEEKS. THERE WAS A SECTION ABOUT ASH.”

Ben winced. “Now I feel bad.”

“You always feel bad.”

“He burned nine kingdoms.”

“Allegedly.”

“I CAN HEAR YOU.”

Sana checked her watch. “If we leave now, we can still make the late class.”

June looked at the burning cathedral, the hysterical sirens, and the ancient horror sitting in the fountain. Somewhere below, the city guard had arrived and was trying to subdue Vethrak with a net clearly labeled **FOR GARGOYLES ONLY**.

For the first time all evening, June smiled.

“Do you think they’ll let us keep the aprons?”

---

They were bad at pottery.

Not heroically bad. Not bad in a way that concealed a secret gift. They were simply awful.

Ben made a bowl that could also be used as evidence. Sana’s vase leaned so far to one side that the instructor moved it away from the edge of the table. June spent twenty minutes trying to center a lump of clay and instead centered herself into a state of profound personal rage.

“This is wonderful,” she said.

The instructor patted her shoulder. “You’ll get there.”

“No, I won’t.”

“Probably not,” Ben agreed.

June’s clay flew off the wheel and struck the wall with a wet smack.

All three of them burst out laughing.

Then June’s phone buzzed. A red alert flashed across the screen:

**CITYWIDE EMERGENCY. UNIDENTIFIED ENTITY IN THE OLD AQUEDUCT. ALL AVAILABLE PERSONNEL—**

Ben and Sana looked at her.

June looked at the message, then at the shapeless gray disaster under her hands.

She turned the phone face down.

“Give it ten minutes,” she said. “I’m finally doing something I don’t know how to do.”

## No One Serves Forever

The first thing Lieutenant Mara Voss did at Kestrel Station was count the living.

There were seven, including herself.

The second thing she did was count the dead.

There were forty-one, and Command wanted every one of them.

“Hospital train *Mercy Nine* is twenty-two minutes out,” said the colonel over the radio. “Eight hundred wounded aboard. Enemy armor will reach the station in ten. Hold the eastern platform until the train clears the switch.”

Voss looked along the platform. Roof fallen in. Windows gone. One machine gun with half a belt of ammunition. Beyond the broken signal gantry, gray shapes moved through the smoke.

“Understood,” she said.

On her collar she wore the crossed rifle and key of Special Division Infantry, Necromancer Class. The field manual described her duties as *battlefield personnel recovery*.

The manual had been written by someone who had never heard a dead friend ask for a cigarette.

Voss knelt beside the nearest body.

Sergeant Anik Dey had been killed by shrapnel beneath the station clock. His rifle lay across his chest, and someone had folded his hands over it. Voss remembered him doing the same thing for other soldiers at three different sieges.

She unbuttoned his collar and found his identity tag.

Corporal Sen watched from the machine-gun nest. “How many can you raise?”

“All of them.”

Sen glanced at the bodies. “Then why are you asking?”

Because there were two ways to call back the dead.

You could invite the soul, or you could put a hook through it and pull.

The second method was faster.

Voss pressed the tag between her palms. Silver wire glimmered around her wrist.

“Sergeant Anik Dey,” she said. “Will you stand?”

Cold moved through the station. The dead man opened his eyes.

For a moment he simply stared at the ruined ceiling. Then he turned his head.

“Voss?”

“Yes, Sergeant.”

“You look like hell.”

“There’s a hospital train coming. We need to hold the platform.”

Dey considered this. He looked at the sky visible through the roof, pale with approaching dawn.

“All right,” he said.

He sat up.

Voss moved to the next body.

Some of the dead said yes. Some asked whether the enemy was still winning. One wanted to know if his brother had made it out. Voss answered when she could and admitted when she couldn’t.

Private Saye, nineteen years old, with a rifle hole beneath his chin, said no.

“Rest,” Voss told him, and closed his eyes.

In the end, eighteen stood.

Twenty-three remained where they had fallen.

Dey took charge of the station gun. The other dead infantry filled gaps in the barricade, carrying ammunition, dragging wreckage, uncovering a mortar tube buried beneath a ticket kiosk. They worked without complaint, though not without comment.

“I’ve been killed twice this month,” complained a woman named Ors, searching her pockets. “Has anyone seen my lighter?”

“You only died once,” said Sen.

“Then it’s been a very bad month.”

The enemy arrived before the smoke cleared.

The first shell struck the station hotel. The second took off the clock tower. Then infantry came through the eastern fog in open order, rifles flashing.

Dey’s machine gun began to speak.

Voss lay behind a toppled baggage cart and fired between its wheels. Around her, the raised soldiers fought with the economy of people who had already spent their fear. A burst caught Ors across the chest; she looked down, swore, and kept feeding the mortar. A dead corporal lost most of one leg and continued passing ammunition from where he sat.

Every wound reached Voss as a tug on the silver wire.

Every destroyed body cut a thread.

By the fifteenth minute, the enemy had reached the signal gantry.

By the eighteenth, Dey’s gun was empty.

The radio crackled. “Voss, this is Command. Enact full requisition.”

She looked at the twenty-three unrisen.

“No.”

A pause.

“That was not a request, Lieutenant. Reactivate all available assets.”

Private Saye’s face was very still beneath his covered eyes.

Voss keyed the transmitter. “They’re not available.”

Dey appeared beside the baggage cart, carrying the demolition satchel.

“How long?” he asked.

Voss checked her watch. “Four minutes.”

He looked toward the eastern arcade. Its brick supports ran over the drainage culvert—the last covered approach into the station. Enough explosive in the right place would bring the whole arcade down.

Sen saw it too. “That’ll buy us four minutes.”

“It’ll buy us more,” Dey said. “It’ll take them ten to dig through.”

Voss did not offer him the satchel.

Dey held out his hand.

“You don’t have to,” she said.

“Neither did you.” He nodded toward Private Saye. “That’s why I’m doing it.”

Voss gave him the satchel.

Dey started away, then stopped.

“When you write the report, don’t make it sound noble. I just want to get off shift.”

“I’ll put that in.”

“Liar.”

He disappeared into the arcade.

The explosion lifted the platform beneath Voss’s boots. Brick and iron vanished inside a brown cloud. The eastern barricade collapsed, and with it the enemy’s covered approach. Rifle fire faltered. Somewhere beyond the station, a train whistle sounded.

Once.

Twice.

Three long notes.

Clear passage.

The raised soldiers who remained lowered their weapons.

Voss released them one at a time.

Ors went first, still complaining about her lighter. The others followed, sinking gratefully into stillness as Voss spoke their names and closed her hand around each silver thread.

There was no thread left for Dey.

When it was finished, the radio crackled again.

“Voss. Report.”

She picked up the handset.

“The station held. *Mercy Nine* is clear.”

“And the remaining assets?”

Voss looked at the twenty-three bodies she had refused to raise.

“Released.”

“You were ordered to use every available body.”

“I did,” she said. “Every available body volunteered.”

Silence hissed over the channel.

Then: “You’ll answer for this.”

Voss set the handset down.

Around her, the dead lay among the spent cartridges and broken bricks. She sat beside Sergeant Dey’s empty machine gun and listened to the hospital train fading into the distance.

No voices.

No orders.

No one calling muster.

Just the dead, allowed at last to be dead.

### The Third Bell

Voss’s first blow numbed Tamsin’s sword arm. His second drove her back against the sluice wheel.

Iron spokes pressed into her spine. Beneath the grated floor, the reservoir muttered in the dark, patient and enormous.

“Move,” Voss said.

Two bells had rung over the city. When the third sounded, the lower streets would be empty. Until then, Tamsin had to keep the gate closed.

“The flood will stop the army at the bridge,” Voss said. “You know that.”

“There are still people down there.”

“I know.”

He came on.

His thrust should have taken her through the throat. She twisted around the wheel, and his point sparked against iron. She cut at his wrist; he turned the blade aside and nearly took her fingers with the riposte.

He had taught her every form she used. Worse, he had taught her when to abandon them.

Tamsin tried the broken-feint he had once beaten into her for relying on too often. He was waiting. His pommel cracked against her mouth. She stumbled, spat blood, and caught his next cut on the edge of her sword. The shock buckled her knees.

He was stronger. He was fresher. And he was not yet trying to kill her.

That last advantage disappeared when she opened his cheek.

Voss touched the blood, looked at it, and stopped offering warnings.

His next attack drove her halfway around the wheel. She blocked high, low, then high again, each parry slower than the last. There was no space to think, only the white rasp of steel and the growing burn in her lungs. Her heel struck the chain coiled beside the mechanism. She went down on one knee.

Voss kicked the sword from her hand.

It skidded across the stone and stopped against the far wall.

For a moment, neither of them moved. Tamsin knelt with her empty hands raised. Blood ran warm along her ribs.

“You can’t stop water with a dead woman,” he said.

“No.”

He turned to the wheel.

Her sword was too far away. The iron locking pin lay at her feet, where Voss had thrown it after drawing it from the gate. She snatched it up and charged.

It was not a form he had taught her. There was no grace in it, no defense, nothing but the few steps between them and the wheel beginning to turn.

Voss looked back.

She swung the pin at his head. He ducked and cut her across the side. Pain erased the chamber. She hit him anyway, shoulder to breastplate, and they crashed against the wheel together. The chain jumped. Somewhere below, the gate lifted an inch and stopped.

Voss seized her by the coat and hurled her down.

She caught his wrist as she fell. Not to hold him—she knew she couldn’t—but to pull him close enough that his killing stroke went wide. His sword punched through stone beside her ear.

She drove the locking pin into the gap beneath his knee.

Voss grunted and staggered. Tamsin scrambled up, got one hand on the wheel, and forced the pin back into its slot.

His blade entered her side.

This time there was no numbness. Only a deep, astonishing cold.

Voss’s face was very near hers. His hand rested on the hilt between them. He could have withdrawn the sword. He did not.

“Enough,” he said quietly.

Tamsin’s fingers were locked around his sleeve. Her legs had begun to shake, but she kept herself between him and the mechanism.

He looked toward the city.

The third bell began to ring.

Its voice rolled over the rooftops, deep and slow. Voss closed his eyes. Tamsin let go of his sleeve.

“There,” she whispered. “You can have the gate.”

He caught her before she struck the floor.

Behind him, the wheel began to turn. Chains rattled through their housings, and the reservoir gave a long, hollow groan. Water thundered into the lower streets, swallowing courtyards, markets, stairways, doors.

Voss held his cloak against her wound with both hands.

The water took the city, street by street.

It did not take a single scream with it.

content:
## Until the First Flower

Death came for Elsie Wren on a Tuesday in October, at seventeen minutes past four.

He found her in the garden, arguing with a bulb.

“No,” she was saying. “You go in the ground. That’s the entire arrangement.”

Death consulted his paper.

**ELSIE WREN. 4:17 P.M.**

There was no mention of gardening.

“You’re standing on my trowel,” she said.

Death moved.

Elsie was eighty-one, with soil in the creases of her hands and a blue cardigan buttoned wrong. She looked him over without the least courtesy.

“You look cold.”

“I am often told I look inevitable.”

“That too. Pass me the bag.”

Death passed her the bag.

“I have come for you,” he said.

“Yes, I gathered. You’ll have to wait.”

She pressed the last bulb into the earth, then sat back on her heels and winced. Death saw the pain move through her. He saw, too, the careful way she hid it. People often thought pain made them difficult to read. To Death, it made them transparent.

“There,” Elsie said. “Now it’s done.”

He held out his hand.

She looked at the freshly turned soil. “They’re crocuses.”

Death waited.

“I’ve never planted the blue ones before. The packet says they’ll come up in March, but packets are optimistic by nature.”

“Elsie.”

“I should like to see whether they do.”

There was a procedure for refusal. There was a procedure for bargaining, weeping, raging, and pretending not to be at home. There was no procedure for crocuses.

“Until the first flower,” Death said.

Elsie smiled. “You’d better hope it isn’t that one. It went in sideways.”

Between October and March, Death visited eleven times.

Officially, he came to inspect the bulbs.

On the second visit, Elsie made him tea. He held the cup until it went cold, then drank it anyway because she seemed disappointed.

“What does it taste like?” she asked.

“Being told to sit down.”

“That’s chamomile.”

On the fourth visit, she gave him a scarf.

On the sixth, he arrived with his black coat torn at the elbow and stood in her kitchen while she mended it with green thread.

“It was a rosebush,” he said.

“I wasn’t going to ask.”

“You were.”

“I was hoping it was something more interesting. A duel, perhaps.”

Death considered the thousands of years behind him: battlefields and bedrooms, sea roads and sickrooms, all the doors through which he had passed without knocking.

“No one has ever sewn my coat before.”

“No one’s ever had you standing long enough in their kitchen.”

She bit off the thread. Then, because a loose blue button had come away from her cardigan, she sewed that to the inside of his cuff.

“There,” she said. “Something bright.”

Death wore it beneath his sleeve for the rest of the winter.

Elsewhere, he continued his work. He collected a king who apologized to his servants, a baby whose mother would not let go, and an old soldier who laughed and said, *There you are.* He came to Elsie afterward with snow on his shoulders and found her asleep beside the fire.

He stood watching her breathe.

He had watched people breathe before. He had never found it necessary to pay attention.

“Are you tired?” she asked without opening her eyes.

“No.”

“You look tired.”

Death sat down.

After a while, he said, “Perhaps.”

Elsie reached over and patted his hand.

By February, the pain had begun stealing whole days from her. Death could delay an ending, but he could not make her body young. He could not return the garden to her knees or take the ache from her bones. He discovered that there were many things he could not do, and that knowing them was worse than being cold.

One evening he said, “I believe I love you.”

Elsie was winding wool into a ball. The wool stopped turning.

“Yes,” she said.

Death frowned. “Is that all?”

“It’s a considerable thing to believe.” She set the wool aside. “Come here.”

He came.

She took his face between her hands. Her palms smelled of soap and dried lavender.

“I love you too, you great sombre creature. That’s why you mustn’t make it into something cruel.”

“I could keep you here.”

“No. You could keep yourself here. That isn’t the same.”

“You don’t have to die.”

“Everyone has to die.”

“Not if I don’t take you.”

For the first time, she looked angry.

“And what would you be keeping? Soon I won’t be able to get down the path. Then I won’t remember the names of the flowers. Then I’ll stop looking forward to your knock at the door. Don’t make me spend what’s left of myself persuading you to be kind.”

Death looked away.

On the windowsill, the blue button glimmered at his cuff.

“I don’t know how,” he said.

Elsie’s anger softened.

“Yes, you do. You’ve done it for everyone else. Just stay with me.”

The first crocus opened on a raw morning in March.

It was purple, not blue, and slightly crooked.

Death brought it indoors in a small glass. Elsie was in bed by then, propped among pillows, her cardigan folded over a chair. Beyond the window, the garden was colorless except for that single flower.

She studied it gravely.

“Well,” she said. “The packet lied.”

“Yes.”

“Worth waiting for?”

“No.”

She laughed, and the laugh turned into a cough. Death waited until it passed.

Then he said, “Yes.”

Elsie looked at him.

He sat beside her and took her hand. He did not hold out his own in the old way, palm open, patient as a doorway. He simply held hers.

“I don’t want to,” he said.

“I know.”

“I shall miss you.”

“That’s the trouble with being loved. Someone always does.”

Outside, the wind moved through the bare branches. The little crocus trembled in its glass.

Elsie squeezed his fingers.

“Stay,” she whispered.

So Death stayed.

For the first time in his endless existence, he closed his eyes while he worked.

What happened next belonged to Elsie, and he never told anyone. When he returned to himself, the room was very quiet. Her hand was still in his, but it was only a hand now: small, cool, and mortal.

Death sat with her until evening.

Afterward, he did something he had never done. He kept an appointment beyond its proper hour. He sat at her kitchen table and drank a cup of tea. It tasted of chamomile and salt, though he had added no salt.

Years passed.

Death continued to knock, though he did not always need doors. He learned to sit when the dying asked him to sit. He learned that gentleness did not lessen grief, but sometimes gave it somewhere to rest.

And every autumn, in a garden behind a little house that eventually belonged to other people, he planted bulbs.

The new owners could never explain why crocuses appeared each spring in places they had not planted them: beneath the window, beside the path, once in a neat purple circle around the doorstep.

Death kept the blue button sewn inside his cuff.

He had come to collect a life and had been given, briefly, a place in it.

It was not enough.

It was everything.

content:
### Support Class

For as long as I could remember, my life had a soundtrack.

Not songs with lyrics. Scores. Soft piano when I was alone, warm strings at weddings, an anxious little violin figure whenever I waited for medical results. My first kiss had arrived with a tentative waltz. My second had used the same waltz, but with a bassoon doing something sarcastic underneath it.

No one else could hear it. I knew because, at age seven, I’d asked my teacher to please turn down the drums during a spelling test.

The music didn’t predict the future. It only told me what sort of scene I was in, which was occasionally useful and often just rude.

When my father died, it went silent for three days.

So I trusted it.

That Tuesday, I went to the grocery store with six items on my list and a coupon for yogurt I had no intention of using. I was debating whether pasta counted as dinner if you ate it directly from the pot when the music stopped.

Then the drums came in.

Aggressive synth brass followed, along with a bass line climbing the same four notes and an arpeggio so frantic it sounded late for work. It was heroic, urgent, and completely devoid of personality.

The most generic JRPG battle theme I had ever heard.

It looped after forty seconds. Seamlessly.

I stood very still beside the canned tomatoes.

A woman compared two jars of mayonnaise. Someone’s child kicked the side of a freezer. At the front of the store, a cashier dragged a scanner across a loaf of bread with the weariness of a man dismantling explosives.

No swords. No monsters. No flashing red eyes.

I looked down at my basket.

Milk. Coffee. Pasta. A lemon.

None of these were weapons.

“Oh, good,” said someone behind me. “You hear it.”

I turned.

An elderly woman stood in the aisle wearing a yellow raincoat and orthopedic shoes. Her silver hair was braided down her back. In one hand she held a shopping list. In the other was a canvas grocery bag printed with the words **APPRECIATE TEACHERS**.

“Hear what?” I asked.

She gave me a look of such profound disappointment that I immediately revised my answer.

“The battle music.”

Her expression improved. She reached into the canvas bag and pulled out a sword.

Not a fantasy sword with jewels and a name. A plain, practical sword, the sort of sword that had probably been purchased because the family’s old sword had finally worn out.

“Who are you?” I said.

“Marjorie. Take this.”

She handed me a ten-pound bag of salt.

“Why?”

“Questions after the encounter.”

Something splashed in the produce section.

The mayonnaise woman lowered her jars. The child stopped kicking the freezer.

A blue slime oozed out from beneath the display of watermelons.

It was roughly the size of an ottoman, translucent, and wearing a tiny golden crown.

I stared at it.

“You have got to be kidding me.”

“Don’t judge by the model,” Marjorie said. “Judge by the hit points.”

The slime opened a mouth.

That was unfair, I felt. Slimes should not have been able to do that.

It lunged.

The battle theme shrieked upward, and some instinct made me grab Marjorie’s raincoat and pull. We stumbled backward as the slime struck the floor where she’d been standing. Watermelons exploded. A sign advertising locally sourced cantaloupe spun into the air.

Marjorie swung her sword. The blade struck the slime’s side and sank six inches before stopping.

The slime shivered.

The sword bounced out.

“Right,” Marjorie said. “One of those.”

It lunged again. I swung the bag of salt.

The bag tore.

Salt erupted across the aisle in a white, glittering cloud. The slime recoiled, smoking around the edges, and for one hopeful second I thought I had discovered its elemental weakness.

Then it sucked up the salt and doubled in size.

“No,” Marjorie said. “You’ve seasoned it.”

The cashier was shouting. Shoppers ran toward the doors. The slime rolled after them, crushing a display of crackers.

I threw my lemon.

It vanished into the slime without a trace.

Marjorie seized my sleeve. “Stop trying to do damage.”

“What else am I supposed to do?”

“Your job.”

“I don’t have a job!”

“You do now. Listen.”

The music pounded in my ears. Brass, drums, that ridiculous bass line. Beneath it all, I noticed a pattern I hadn’t heard before: three quick beats, a rest, then a low note like a door closing underground.

The slime drew itself upward.

Three quick beats.

“Left!” I shouted.

Marjorie stepped left.

The slime slammed down on her right, hard enough to crack the tiles.

The music repeated.

“Back!”

We retreated. A wave of blue jelly swept through the space between us.

Marjorie looked at me with new interest.

“There it is,” she said.

“There what is?”

“Your job.”

The slime surged again. This time I heard the cymbal before it moved and pulled her clear without being told.

For thirty-two years, my soundtrack had been something that happened to me. A narrator. A warning light. A joke at my expense.

Now, as Marjorie raised her sword and the slime gathered itself for another attack, I heard an empty space beneath the melody.

Not silence. A gap.

Something waiting.

I clapped on the beat.

The drums grew louder.

I clapped again, then hummed the bass line. It was idiotic. It was four notes. It sounded like an introduction to a song no one had bothered finishing.

A trumpet appeared above my humming.

Then another.

The brass braided itself into something sharper. Marjorie’s shoulders straightened. Her sword rose exactly with the rhythm.

“Oh,” she said softly. “You’re a quick study.”

The slime’s crown flashed.

The music changed.

The drums dropped out. A cold, high string note slid beneath the brass.

I didn’t know what the change meant, but I knew I hated it.

“It’s doing something,” I said.

“Extremely helpful.”

The slime flattened itself against the floor. Blue tendrils shot outward, slipping beneath shelves and around our ankles. The whole building groaned. Freezer doors flew open. Lights flickered.

The string note climbed higher.

Marjorie tried to pull her foot free and couldn’t.

The slime began dragging her toward its mouth.

I caught her wrists.

“Any time now,” she said.

“I’m thinking!”

“Think rhythmically.”

The melody was collapsing. The strings had taken over, thin and shrill, and the battle theme was becoming something slower. Hungrier.

So I stopped humming the bass line.

Instead, I hummed the little tune I used to hum when I was nervous as a child. Something my father had made up while washing dishes. It had no name and barely a melody. He used to perform it with tremendous seriousness while holding a plate like a microphone.

For one terrifying moment, nothing happened.

Then the soundtrack laughed.

I swear it did.

A piano picked up my father’s tune. The drums stumbled, found the new tempo, and followed. The horns came back wrong-footed, tried to resume their pompous little loop, and were swept aside by an enormous, joyful saxophone.

Marjorie grinned.

“There you are.”

The tendrils loosened.

She tore one foot free, then the other. I kept humming, louder now, clapping whenever I remembered and shouting whenever I didn’t. The slime shuddered. Its crown tilted.

The music raced toward a crescendo.

I heard it eight beats before it arrived.

“Marjorie,” I said.

She lifted the sword.

“Wait.”

The slime opened its mouth.

“Wait.”

The crown blazed gold.

“Now.”

Her blade struck it.

The victory fanfare was obnoxiously short.

Three triumphant notes, a cymbal crash, and silence.

The slime burst. Not violently—more like a water balloon losing an argument. Blue mist filled the produce section. When it cleared, there was no sign of the creature except for several damp watermelons and a small golden object ringing against the floor.

The object rolled to my shoe.

I picked it up.

A coupon.

Seventy-five cents off laundry detergent.

Marjorie inspected it. “Not bad.”

“We nearly died.”

“Yes, but detergent’s expensive.”

The cashier approached, surveyed the aisle, and sighed.

“If that was another crowned one,” he said, “you’re paying for the peas.”

“Put them on my tab,” Marjorie told him.

I looked from her to the sword to the ruined produce section.

“What,” I said carefully, “is happening?”

Marjorie slid the sword back into the teachers’ bag.

“You’re support.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It’s the only one you’re getting before coffee.”

We found my coffee three aisles over. My milk had survived. The pasta was fine. The lemon was gone, presumably forever.

At the register, Marjorie took my receipt and wrote a phone number on the back. Beneath it she added:

**THURSDAY. WEAR COMFORTABLE SHOES.**

“What’s Thursday?” I asked.

“Hopefully nothing. That’s why I shop on Thursdays.”

Outside, rain had polished the parking lot silver. Marjorie lifted her canvas bag onto one shoulder and raised a hand in farewell.

My soundtrack began again.

Not battle music. Not the thin, cautious piano that usually followed me through my weekdays. Something new: a walking drumbeat, a bright piano figure, and beneath it, almost shyly, my father’s dishwashing tune.

For the first time in my life, the music didn’t feel like it was scoring a scene I was merely watching.

It felt like it was listening back.

I put the receipt in my pocket.

Then I stepped into the rain, humming along.

content:
# The Most Beautiful Woman in the World

No one could agree about her eyes.

To the baker, they were green as sea glass. To the king’s envoy, they were black and sorrowful. A shepherd swore they were gold, while two sisters who had traveled forty miles to see her wept and said they were precisely the blue of their mother’s.

Everyone agreed, however, that Sera was the most beautiful woman in the world.

Kings sent proposals. Poets sent verses, most of them dreadful. A prince crossed a desert with a pearl the size of a pigeon’s egg and had to be carried home after she declined to come to the door.

At last the king announced that he would marry her. Since he had not yet seen her himself, he commissioned Mara, the finest portrait painter in the kingdom, to capture Sera’s likeness for the wedding tapestry.

Mara found Sera in a palace room with tall windows and twelve mirrors, all covered with sheets.

Sera turned as Mara entered.

Mara dropped her charcoal.

“Nell?” she whispered.

Sera’s expression softened. “Not Nell, I’m afraid.”

Mara gripped the edge of a table. Before her stood her sister, who had died at fourteen: the same narrow face, the same impatient mouth, the same small crease between her brows.

“Ah,” said Sera. “A sister. Those are difficult.”

“You knew?”

“Everyone sees someone. The king’s envoy called me Mother and cried into his hat. It made the journey rather awkward.”

Mara looked away. “I can’t paint you.”

“That’s what the last three painters said.”

“What happened to them?”

“The king had their beards shaved off. Fortunately, you haven’t got one.”

Despite herself, Mara laughed.

Sera smiled. “There. We’ve made progress.”

Mara unpacked her brushes.

For the first week, she painted Nell. Nell sitting by the window. Nell holding a book. Nell with sunlight in her hair.

But Sera would not sit properly. She slouched. She kicked off her shoes beneath her gown. When she thought a joke was especially funny, she laughed before reaching the end of it and had to begin again.

Nell had never done that.

Sera hated plums, loved thunder, and could mend a torn sleeve so neatly that the stitches seemed to vanish. She was kind to servants and merciless at cards. She had a small white scar on her chin, which she had received falling out of a cherry tree after insisting she could climb higher than her brother.

Mara began drawing the scar.

Then the hands, ink-stained at the fingertips.

Then the uneven mouth.

One morning Sera asked, “What do you see?”

Mara studied her.

“Brown eyes,” she said. “The left one opens a little wider than the right. Your hair is nearly black, except where the sun has touched it. You have a scar on your chin. And there is a crease here”—she touched her own brow—“because you are trying not to look pleased.”

Sera was very still.

“Say it again,” she said.

So Mara did.

The finished portrait showed a woman seated beside an open window. She wore no crown and held no flowers. There was a mended sleeve beside her and a half-eaten apple on the sill. She looked as though someone had just said something ridiculous and she was waiting for them to realize it.

When the king saw the painting, he was silent for a long time.

“This,” he said at last, “is a joke.”

“No, Your Majesty,” said Mara. “A joke would have taken less time.”

The king called her a fraud. He called Sera a fraud as well, though he still had not met her. The wedding was canceled, the pearl prince sent a triumphant letter, and Mara and Sera were ordered to leave the capital before sunset.

At the city gate, Sera lifted her veil.

The guard immediately fell to one knee and addressed her by the name of his childhood sweetheart.

Sera lowered the veil again.

“Will it ever stop?” she asked as they walked out onto the road.

“Kings, perhaps,” said Mara. “Fools, never.”

They traveled until they reached a village where no one had heard of Sera, though this took longer than either expected. There Sera opened a shop mending books, and Mara painted farmers, weddings, dogs, and the occasional uncooperative child.

Strangers still sometimes entered the shop and forgot why they had come. But those who stayed long enough began to notice other things: that Sera always saved the cracked bindings for herself, that she sang badly while working, that she could identify a book’s owner by the stains on its pages.

Gradually, they stopped calling her beautiful and started calling her Sera.

Years passed. The world found several other women to call the most beautiful.

When Sera was seventy-nine, Mara painted her one last time. Her hair was white, her hands were bent, and the crease between her brows had settled in permanently.

Sera looked at the finished portrait for a long while.

“Well?” Mara asked.

“There I am,” said Sera.

She smiled. In the painting, she was already smiling back.

content:
## The Human Gallery

When the Museum of Near and Far announced its exhibition on terrestrial humanity, forty-one worlds submitted portraits.

No two gave humans the same number of limbs.

This was not entirely humanity’s fault.

Earth had been silent for six hundred and eleven years. Its oceans, cities, and bones lay beyond the reach of any ship then living, but its signals had crossed the dark for centuries: music, arguments, mathematical proofs, recipes, declarations of war, apologies, weather reports, and an astonishing quantity of material concerning the private habits of cats.

From this evidence, each world had made its reconstruction.

Young Tavi visited the exhibition with Curator Ilex, hoping to choose an image for the school’s annual Festival of Otherness.

The first portrait came from the ocean philosophers of Pelag. It was a transparent globe filled with salt water. Inside floated a delicate white tree.

“A human,” Ilex explained, “was thought to be an ocean that grew a scaffold and learned to walk.”

Tavi peered into the globe. “Did they have no skin?”

“Pelag considered skin philosophically unlikely.”

The next portrait, contributed by the mathematicians of Aether, consisted only of a speaker. From it came a rising and falling tone.

“They believed humans were patterns of compression in an invisible medium,” said Ilex.

“Were they right?”

“Partially. Humans called them voices.”

“Then where were their bodies?”

“Aether considered bodies an unfounded elaboration.”

They moved on.

The six-legged sculptors of Keth had cast a human in bronze. It leaned forward at a precarious angle, long arms flung out, neither foot quite touching the ground.

The title was **Walking: A Method of Continuously Almost Falling**.

Tavi studied it for some time.

“That one,” they said, “looks correct.”

In the Hall of Interpretive Confidence stood the more alarming works.

One world, having received three centuries of Earth’s news broadcasts but none of its entertainment, portrayed humanity as a mouth filled with flags. Another depicted a human mother as a many-eyed creature crouched over a nest of smaller humans, all of them screaming.

“She is expressing affection,” said Ilex.

“Are you certain?”

“No.”

The machine civilization of Orro had sent the exhibition’s largest piece: a golden, winged being with one circular eye and limbs of antennae.

“They mistook a spacecraft for the human,” Ilex said. “And the human for a detachable component used during repairs.”

Tavi looked at the graceful metal figure. “Were they offended when corrected?”

“They sent a revised model with two spacecraft.”

At last they reached the final gallery.

It contained no portrait. Only a bench, a small receiver, and a plaque:

**PRIMARY MATERIAL. ARTISTS ARE ASKED NOT TO IMPROVE IT.**

Tavi sat. Ilex switched on the receiver.

First came static.

Then a voice said, “Hello from the children of planet Earth.”

There followed a confusion of sounds. Wind. Thunder. A sudden bright cascade of notes. Something barking. Something singing. A locomotive. A heartbeat. A burst of laughter so brief and unguarded that Tavi leaned toward the speaker.

Then came greetings in languages no living tongue could pronounce.

Some were formal. Some hesitant. One speaker seemed to be smiling. Another paused halfway through, as if uncertain whether anyone would truly hear.

The recording ended.

“Which one was human?” Tavi asked.

“Scholars disagree.”

“But you must know something about their appearance.”

“We know they had hands,” said Ilex. “They mentioned them often. They put them together when pleased, raised them when surrendering, extended them when meeting, and used them to make both tools and music.”

“So draw the hands.”

“Which ones?”

Tavi looked back toward the entrance. Through the successive doorways they could see the salt-water globe, the leaning bronze figure, the golden spacecraft, and the terrible mouth full of flags.

“They all drew themselves,” Tavi said.

Ilex’s outer eyes closed, which was the nearest their species came to smiling.

“All portraits contain the portraitist.”

“Then why exhibit them?”

Ilex took a moment to answer.

“Because before we heard Earth, every world represented here believed it was alone. Afterward, we began listening for one another.”

For the Festival of Otherness, Tavi did not copy any of the portraits.

Instead, they drew the museum’s final gallery. Around the little receiver they placed Pelagic philosophers, Aether mathematicians, Keth sculptors, Orro machines, and beings from all the other worlds. Each looked different. Each heard something different. All were listening.

There were no humans in the picture.

Ilex examined it carefully.

“You have drawn us.”

“Yes.”

“Then why call it **Terrestrial Humans**?”

“Because before them,” Tavi said, “we weren’t all in the same room.”

The drawing was hung in the final gallery, opposite the receiver. Visitors often stood before it longer than they stood before any other piece.

Beneath the title, in Tavi’s small, uneven script, was a single additional line:

**Unfinished. We are still listening.**

prompt: Your body morphs every night , you alternate every day as a man and a woman . You try to slip out of your one-night stand 's apartment before he wakes up to see the transformation .
content:
### The Hour Between

The dress was the first problem.

It had looked elegant on me last night: dark green, low enough in the back to make Daniel forget the name of the song playing in the bar. Now it lay over his desk chair like a shed skin, and in less than an hour it would fit me about as well as it would fit the chair.

The second problem was Daniel.

He slept with one arm flung across my side of the bed, his face buried in the pillow. Every time I shifted, he made a small, displeased sound and pulled the blanket closer.

I eased backward an inch at a time.

4:08, according to the microwave in the kitchen.

The change usually started around five. Sometimes earlier, if I was tired. Sometimes later, if I had crossed time zones, though never later enough to be useful. I had tried sleeping pills, blackout curtains, and once a flight from Vancouver to Tokyo. My body kept its own calendar.

Woman one day. Man the next. No skipping, no pausing, no extra day for good behavior.

Daniel’s arm slid off the mattress.

I froze.

He snored.

I rolled free, caught my dress as it slipped from the chair, and located one shoe beneath the bed. The other was in the living room, standing upright inside a potted ficus.

“Subtle,” I whispered to it.

My phone had twelve percent battery. My earrings were in my coat pocket. My coat was hanging by the door. All that remained was to retrieve the shoe, put on enough clothing to avoid arrest, and get downstairs before my skeleton began rearranging the furniture.

Last night, Daniel had asked whether I wanted to come up for a drink.

“I don’t usually do this,” I had told him.

He had considered that seriously. “Drink?”

“Go home with strangers.”

“Ah.” He’d smiled. “Me neither, except when I do.”

It was a terrible line. I had liked him immediately.

In the living room, the ficus gave up my shoe without a fight. I was pulling on my coat when the first ache arrived behind my knees.

I checked the microwave through the open doorway.

4:31.

Early.

“No,” I said.

My fingers tingled. A deep, familiar pressure gathered along my spine.

Not here. Not in a strange apartment with navy sheets, three guitars, and a man who had kissed me as if kissing were something he had been meaning to get around to all his life.

I made it to the door.

The chain slid from its track with a small metallic sigh.

My hand slipped on the deadbolt.

“Ari?”

Daniel’s voice was thick with sleep.

“Go back to bed.”

It came out wrong—my voice catching halfway between registers.

The bedroom floor creaked.

I yanked at the deadbolt, but my fingers had begun to lengthen around it. Pain flashed through my wrists. I dropped my shoe.

Daniel appeared in the doorway, shirtless, hair standing up on one side.

For a moment we simply looked at each other.

Then my shoulders moved.

It wasn’t violent. There was no tearing, no blood, none of the things people imagined when I made the mistake of explaining. It was more like being carefully argued with. My body proposed one shape, then another. Bone followed bone. Muscle revised its position. My height rose by degrees until the coat pulled tight across my back.

Daniel’s eyes widened.

“Don’t,” I said.

He stopped. “Don’t what?”

“Anything yet.”

“Okay.”

He sat down on the floor.

That was so unexpected that I almost laughed, but the laugh became a gasp as my jaw changed. I gripped the back of a chair and waited. Daniel stared at his hands. He did not run. He did not reach for his phone. He did not say my name again in that careful tone people used when they wanted to check whether it was still safe to know you.

After a while, the pain receded.

The apartment came back into focus: the ticking radiator, the ficus, the green dress pooled over my arm. I was taller now. Broader. Daniel’s coat hung ridiculously from my shoulders.

He glanced up, then quickly away.

“There’s a blanket behind you,” he said.

I wrapped it around myself. “You can look.”

“Are you sure?”

“No.”

He looked anyway.

I knew what he saw. Same dark eyes. Same crooked mouth, though the face around it had changed. I had stopped trying to decide which version was real when I was nineteen. Both were real. That was the entire inconvenience.

Daniel swallowed. “Does it hurt?”

“Yes.”

“Every night?”

“Every night.”

“And tomorrow you’ll—”

“Change back.”

He nodded slowly. “Huh.”

I waited.

“That’s it?” I asked.

“I’m working on something better.”

Despite myself, I laughed. This time my voice stayed low.

Daniel stood, keeping a cautious distance, and went into the bedroom. He returned with a gray sweatshirt and a pair of drawstring trousers, which he placed on the arm of the sofa.

“These should fit better than the coat.”

I didn’t move.

He backed into the kitchen. “The kettle’s loud,” he said. “I can make coffee, or I can wait until you’ve gone. Either is fine.”

“You’re being very calm.”

“I sat on the floor because my legs weren’t working.”

That explained it.

I dressed behind the sofa. The trousers were short, but the sweatshirt fit. When I came out, Daniel was measuring coffee into a chipped yellow pot.

He didn’t ask why I hadn’t told him. I was grateful for that, because all my answers sounded unkind when I said them aloud.

Because it was supposed to be one night.

Because I had wanted to be wanted without instructions.

Because leaving first had always seemed easier than watching someone decide what I was.

Daniel poured water into the kettle and set it on the stove.

“You can still leave,” he said.

“I know.”

“I mean, I’d prefer you didn’t feel like you had to escape through the ficus.”

“I was using the door.”

“The ficus looked involved.”

Outside, the windows were beginning to pale. Somewhere below, a delivery truck rattled over a pothole. The ordinary morning noises made me feel more exposed than the transformation had.

I picked up my phone. There was a car six minutes away. I could be home before the sun cleared the buildings. I could leave Daniel with a story he would tell badly for the rest of his life, becoming stranger and stranger with each retelling until I was twelve feet tall and breathing fire.

Or I could stay for twenty minutes.

Not because he had seen me and not run. Not because his kindness entitled him to anything.

Because I was tired.

“Is one of those mugs clean?” I asked.

Daniel looked at the sink. “Define clean.”

I took the least questionable one from the drying rack.

When the coffee was ready, we sat at opposite ends of the sofa. My green dress lay between us. Daniel studied it for a moment, then carefully moved it aside.

“Still Ari?” he asked.

“Still Ari.”

He nodded and handed me the mug.

In the dark window across the room, our reflections hovered over the waking city: Daniel with his disastrous hair, me in borrowed clothes, both of us blurred by steam. I looked like a stranger. I always did, at first.

Daniel’s reflection lifted its cup.

After a moment, mine lifted back.

content:
## Devagar

At 7:12 on Tuesday morning, every president, pope, and hostage negotiator in the world fell silent.

At 7:13, my son asked for the jam, and I thought he was picking a fight.

The first sign was the kitchen wall. WEATHER and SCHOOL appeared as usual, pale blue beside the window. TRANSLATION flickered, turned red, and displayed a message no one had seen before:

**SERVICE INTERRUPTION. NO ESTIMATED RESTORATION TIME.**

For a moment, we all kept chewing.

Then Cátia spoke.

Nothing arrived after it.

Usually her Portuguese came with an English shadow, half a heartbeat behind. The translator preserved her hesitations, her dry little inflections, even the way she sometimes sighed before disagreeing with me. For fourteen years, that shadow had been our marriage’s second language.

Now there was only Portuguese.

I looked at her. She looked at me.

Tomás said something to his sister. Lia answered without taking her eyes off my face. His voice had a small crack near the end of the sentence; hers rose and fell as though she were singing. I had lived with my children for twelve and eight years respectively, and I had never really heard them.

“What?” I said.

Cátia repeated herself.

“No, I—wait.” I tapped the translator behind my ear. Once. Twice. Hard enough that Cátia’s eyebrows lifted.

Tomás spoke faster. Lia pointed past me. All three of them began talking at once.

“One at a time,” I said, though of course that helped no one.

My phone was filling with reports. Summits suspended. Border crossings stalled. Hospitals recruiting anyone who could remember more than please and thank you in a second language. Somewhere, two prime ministers were communicating through drawings.

In our kitchen, Cátia said my name.

Daniel.

That, at least, survived.

The night before, I had come home after Lia was asleep. Again. Cátia had waited for me at this same table, her hands wrapped around a cold cup.

“You keep promising us tomorrow,” she had said.

The translation had been flawless.

I had answered, “Can we not do this now?”

Now, watching her mouth move without understanding a word, I decided she was continuing the argument. Tomás, I decided, was complaining about breakfast. Lia was whining because she sensed the general unhappiness and wanted her share of it.

In the absence of meaning, I supplied my own. It was astonishing how fluently I could misunderstand them.

Then the smoke alarm went off.

Lia was still pointing. Behind me, black smoke curled from the toaster.

Tomás lunged for the plug. Cátia opened the window. I knocked over the coffee trying to help, and Lia rescued the jam with both hands.

For one second, we regarded the little blackened square of toast.

Then Tomás laughed. Not translated laughter—just laughter, an undignified snort he tried to disguise as a cough. Lia laughed at him laughing. Cátia pressed her lips together and failed.

Something in the room loosened.

I put my phone face down.

I sat at the table.

Without sentences to wait for, I began to notice things. Cátia was rubbing her thumb against the side of her finger, which she did when she was anxious. Tomás had butter on his chin. Lia’s socks did not match, and one of them appeared to belong to me.

I made fresh coffee. Cátia’s first: one sugar, no milk. She accepted the cup with both hands.

Breakfast became a series of small proposals.

Cátia held up the bread.

“Pão,” she said.

“Pão,” I repeated.

Tomás lifted an egg.

“Ovo.”

“Ovo.”

Lia, not to be outdone, seized the milk carton.

“Leite,” she announced with such solemnity that I repeated it as though taking an oath.

They slowed down for me. No one had ever needed to slow down before. The translator had made patience unnecessary.

Cátia moved one hand in a gentle circle, as though stirring an enormous, invisible pot.

“Devagar,” she said.

I tried to copy her.

She shook her head, smiling.

“De-va-gar.”

“Devagar.”

Tomás clapped once, sarcastically. Lia kicked him under the table. I knew this because he said, “Ai!” and she looked suddenly fascinated by the ceiling.

Some things, apparently, had never required translation.

From somewhere—the first weekend Cátia and I spent together, perhaps, when I had still believed learning six phrases made me adventurous—I recovered two words.

“Bom dia,” I said.

Her face changed.

Not dramatically. She did not cry. She simply stopped rubbing her finger and looked at me as if I had finally entered the room.

“Bom dia,” she answered.

I looked down at my coffee.

“Desculpa.”

The word did not repair the night before. It did not make me a better husband or explain why I had kept treating my family like something that could be rescheduled. It only located the door.

Cátia put her hand over mine.

Twenty-three minutes after the world stopped understanding itself, the translator chimed.

Tomás was in the middle of a sentence when his English shadow returned.

“—asked for jam, and then the toast caught fire, and you looked at me like I’d declared independence.”

Lia’s shadow said, “You did.”

“I did not.”

“You both did,” Cátia said. “Sit down.”

I stared at Tomás.

“You were asking for jam?”

“Finally,” he said. “The great mystery of our age.”

Cátia’s voice came first in Portuguese, then in English.

“Are you all right?”

“I thought you were angry.”

“I was. Last night. This morning I wanted coffee.”

Tomás reached across me for the jam.

“About last night,” I began.

Cátia raised her other hand and stirred the invisible pot.

“Devagar.”

The translator supplied *slowly*, but her hand was still over mine.

I did not switch the translator off. I had a meeting at nine, Tomás had school, and the world had wars to resume or prevent. But I turned it down while Cátia wrote our new words on the back of a cereal box.

*Pão. Ovo. Desculpa. Devagar.*

Bread. Egg. Sorry. Slowly.

I was late for work. Tomás missed his bus. Lia got jam in her hair and taught me the word for it, though I forgot that one before noon.

By dinner, the world was arguing again in every language. At our table, Cátia held up her cup and waited.

“Devagar,” I said.

She smiled and corrected my pronunciation.

content:
## Pending

At my birth, the midwife wrapped me in a white blanket, pressed my foot onto an ink pad, and gave my mother a gray booklet with no flag on its cover.

**PERSON**, it said.

**CITIZENSHIP: PENDING.**

For eighteen years, *pending* was the longest word I knew.

By law, I could grow up wherever my parents lived. I could attend school, be treated in hospital, and own the ordinary possessions of childhood: a bicycle, a library card, a pair of boots I refused to throw away. But I could not vote, hold public office, or call any border mine.

On my eighteenth birthday, I could name any country in the world, and that country would be required to accept me.

The choice was permanent.

My mother had chosen Ors because, at eighteen, she had admired its constitution. It guaranteed housing, protected journalists, and required every legislator to spend one month each year living on the minimum wage. She had visited Ors only twice, but she still read its newspapers and voted in its elections. Sometimes she grew homesick for streets she had never walked.

My father had chosen Tava, the country where we lived, because his mother was ill and he did not want to leave her.

“I chose a person,” he told me. “She died anyway. The country stayed.”

I intended to be more sensible.

For three years, I kept a notebook. Down the left side of each page I wrote the names of countries. Across the top I ruled columns: healthcare, rainfall, corruption, public transport, press freedom, mountains. I gave extra points for good libraries and deducted them for noisy national anthems.

By the final month, Meridian was winning.

Meridian had clean trains, an independent press, and a prime minister who had resigned after using an official car to move a piano. I admired a country where that counted as a scandal.

Tava, by contrast, had three government ministries housed in one leaking building and a river that entered the city every spring as though checking on property it owned.

“Choose Meridian,” my mother said. “Or Ors. Or somewhere with deserts. Just don’t choose a country to prove you love us.”

My father agreed.

The night before my birthday, the river rose.

We woke to water moving through the kitchen, brown and cold around my ankles. The flood siren should have sounded hours earlier. Instead, the first warning came from Aunt Bea downstairs, who began beating a saucepan with a ladle.

We spent the night carrying people to the upper floors of the school. We found Aunt Bea sitting on her kitchen table with her radio in her lap. My father and two neighbors sandbagged the clinic door. My mother made tea on a camping stove until the gas ran out, after which she continued handing out the mugs because, she said, people behaved better when they were holding something.

The clinic’s roof held.

The siren never sounded.

At dawn, the river withdrew, leaving mud in the streets, a silver fish outside the bakery, and mattresses drying on every wall. A clerk from the water office arrived and explained that the siren’s repair order had been signed eleven months earlier and filed under **Future Improvements**.

I did not look at the damaged city and feel love. There was nothing noble about the mud, nothing beautiful about an old woman’s ruined bedding.

I felt cheated.

That was worse.

If I chose Meridian, I could read about Tava’s floods in the international news. I could feel sorry. I could send money. Choosing Meridian would not make me a coward.

Choosing Tava would not make me good.

That was the annoying thing.

The Choosing Hall had once been a railway station. The departures board still hung above the clerks, though now it listed no destinations, only appointment times.

Ahead of me, a boy I had known since primary school chose a country on the other side of the world and began to cry with relief. No one laughed. Every choice looked sensible from inside the life that had produced it.

Then my name was called.

The clerk was a tired woman with green ink on her fingers. She checked my gray booklet and slid a form across the desk.

“Do you understand that this choice cannot be revoked?”

*No*, I thought.

“Yes,” I said.

“Which country do you wish to be a citizen of?”

I had brought my notebook with me. Meridian’s score was written on the final page, underlined twice.

“Tava,” I said.

The word sounded less like surrender than I had expected, and less like home.

The clerk entered it into her machine. A printer whirred. Somewhere behind the wall, a dog barked. Then she handed me a dark green passport with my photograph inside.

My father made tea when we got home. My mother touched the passport cover once and said, “All right,” in the same voice she used whenever I had made a difficult decision and she intended to help me live with it.

There was a public meeting that evening about the flood sirens.

I went with mud still in the seams of my shoes. The hall smelled of wet coats and disinfectant. The clerk from the water office sat at the front, looking as though he wished the river had taken him instead.

I opened my notebook to a clean page and wrote one question:

**WHO SIGNED THE REPAIR ORDER?**

When the chair asked whether any citizen wished to speak, my hand was shaking.

I raised it anyway.

# Challenging the Behemoth Peak Spider

Everyone who climbed Behemoth Peak to kill its spider carried a longer sword than the last.

Nessa carried a needle.

It was a sailmaker’s needle, long as her hand, and she had used it to mend fishing nets, stitch torn canvas, and sew her father’s climbing harness after he swore it would never hold again. It had held. So had she—until the spider’s web appeared across the headwaters of the River Avel and stopped the water reaching the valley.

By the third day, the mills were silent.

By the sixth, the wells were mud.

On the seventh, Nessa took her father’s knife, threaded her needle with silver cord, and began to climb.

Her father had gone up twelve days before her, carrying an axe and the village’s blessing. Nessa found the axe on the second ridge, buried to its handle in a strand of silk. The silk was thicker than a ship’s mast and trembled with a deep, continuous note, like a harp string plucked by the wind.

Beyond it hung the other challengers.

Knights in split armor. Hunters with bows still clutched in their hands. A wizard whose staff had frozen into a glittering stump. Each was wrapped in white silk, suspended above the abyss.

Nessa did not look long enough to learn whether they were breathing.

She climbed on.

Near the summit, the wind died. The clouds thinned. And the black crag Nessa had mistaken for the peak opened eight red eyes.

The Behemoth Peak Spider unfolded itself from the mountain.

One leg struck the cliff beside her. Stone burst into dust. Nessa swung from her rope, slammed against the rock, and somehow kept hold of the needle.

“Little stitcher,” said the spider. Its voice was the groan of ice under great weight. “Have you come to avenge the river?”

Nessa drew her father’s knife.

“I’ve come to take it back.”

“Then challenge me.”

The words rolled around the summit, ancient and formal.

Nessa looked up at the creature’s armored body, at fangs like fallen towers, and understood that courage was not the absence of fear. Courage was simply what remained when fear had spent itself.

“I challenge you,” she said.

The spider lowered its vast head.

“Accepted. Cut my web, and the river is yours. Fail, and you remain here with the others.”

It drew aside one leg.

Behind it stretched the web.

Nessa had imagined a dam: a white barrier plugging the river’s source. Instead, she saw thousands of strands radiating across the summit, anchored to cliffs on either side. They crossed and recrossed a black fissure in the mountain. Beneath them bulged a lake of meltwater, wide enough to drown the valley.

The web was not holding the river back.

It was holding the mountain together.

Nessa touched the nearest strand. Through it she felt the strain of millions of tons of stone.

“What happened?” she whispered.

“Your people cut too deep for bright stone,” said the spider. “They cracked the frozen heart of the peak. I have been mending it ever since.”

“Why didn’t you tell us?”

“I told the first king who climbed here. He commanded me to move.”

One of the silk-wrapped shapes stirred nearby.

“Nessa?”

Her father’s face emerged from a split in the cocoon. He was gaunt and pale, but alive.

“I cut a strand,” he said. “The mountain started to fall. The spider caught me.” He gave a weak, ashamed laugh. “I’ve had twelve days to consider whether that makes it a poor monster or a very patient one.”

A crack ran through the summit.

The lake boomed behind the web.

One of the spider’s legs buckled. A silver strand snapped with a sound like thunder, and its loose end whipped across the gorge, slicing the top from a pine tree far below.

“Cut the web,” the spider said. There was no mockery in its voice now. Only exhaustion. “Take your river. I am tired of challenging mountains.”

Nessa raised her knife.

Then she turned and cut her own climbing rope.

“Nessa!” her father shouted.

She tied one end around her waist and flung the coil over a lower strand.

“Can you still spin?” she asked the spider.

“Always.”

“Then follow my knots.”

She jumped.

For one terrible instant there was nothing beneath her but cloud and the distant green stitchwork of the valley. Then the rope snapped tight. Nessa swung into the web, caught a strand with both arms, and began to climb.

A net did not fail all at once. Her grandmother had taught her that. It failed one knot at a time.

And it could be saved the same way.

Nessa found the broken junction where three great cables had pulled apart. The spider’s legs were too vast to work there without tearing everything further, but Nessa could fit between the braided fibers. She drove her needle through, silver cord gleaming behind it.

“Left strand to the western spur!” she shouted. “Not the thick one—the one beneath it! Take the strain off the fissure.”

The spider obeyed.

Stone screamed. Water sprayed from the fissure in a glittering plume. Nessa’s fingers tore. Twice she slipped, and twice the spider caught her with the gentlest tip of one leg.

Still she stitched.

When the silver cord ran out, she unthreaded the waistband of her climbing harness. When that was gone, her father, having torn free of his cocoon, crawled along the web and threw her the line from his own.

At last only one gap remained.

Nessa braced herself between two shuddering cables and looked down. Far below lay the valley: dry fields, cold mills, and the pale ribbon of the empty riverbed.

If she failed, there would be no valley to return to.

She took her father’s knife and wedged it beneath the final knot.

“Now,” she said.

The spider pulled.

The knot tightened.

The mountain held.

For a long moment, nothing moved except the clouds drifting peacefully below them.

Then the spider touched one careful claw to a low strand near the river’s source. A narrow opening appeared. Water spilled through it—not a flood, but a clear, singing stream that found the old channel and hurried toward home.

Nessa began to laugh. She could not help it. The sound was small and ragged, but the spider’s eight eyes softened as they watched her.

“You did not cut my web,” it said.

“No.”

“You did not win my challenge.”

Nessa leaned her forehead against the trembling silk.

“Neither did you.”

When Nessa and her father returned to the valley, the river was already turning the mill wheel. People ran to meet them, cheering and weeping. The village elder looked past them at the empty mountain path.

“Where is the spider’s head?” he demanded.

“Holding up the mountain,” Nessa said.

After that, no more champions climbed Behemoth Peak. Instead, once each spring, Nessa went up with coils of rope, pots of pine pitch, and her sailmaker’s needle.

Sometimes her father went with her.

Always, the spider was waiting.

And when children asked how Nessa had defeated the Behemoth Peak Spider, she told them the truth.

“I didn’t. I challenged it to hold on a little longer—and then I helped.”

### The Sunday Biryani

My favourite meal was never served in a restaurant. It arrived every Sunday at my grandmother’s house, in a pot so large that she needed both hands to carry it.

She called it biryani, but to me it seemed more like buried treasure.

When I was ten, she finally allowed me to help. My jobs were important, she said: washing the rice until the water ran clear, picking the brown stems from the mint, and keeping my little brother away from the fried onions. He failed at his job almost immediately.

Grandmother marinated the chicken with yoghurt, garlic, ginger and spices she measured by instinct. A pinch of this. A shake of that. When I asked for the exact amounts, she tapped her chest.

“The recipe is here,” she said.

“But what if I forget?”

“Then you cook until you remember.”

She layered the chicken and rice in the pot, scattering saffron, mint and golden onions between them. Then she sealed the lid with a rope of dough and set it over a low flame.

Waiting was the hardest part.

Slowly, the kitchen changed. First came the warm smell of cinnamon, then cardamom, then the rich, savoury scent of chicken and rice cooking together. The whole house seemed to lean towards the stove. Even my grandfather, who claimed he never ate lunch before two, began setting the table at half past twelve.

At last, Grandmother called me over.

“Carefully,” she said.

I cracked the dough seal. The lid lifted, and a cloud of fragrant steam rose between us. Beneath it lay rice in shades of white, yellow and deep orange, each grain separate and shining. The chicken was tender enough to fall from the bone. Sweet onions clung to the edges, while fresh coriander brightened the top.

We ate it with cool cucumber raita and lemon wedges. The first mouthful was always too hot, but I never learned to wait. There was the softness of the rice, the warmth of the spices, the sharpness of lemon, and then the raita soothing everything again.

Around the table, everyone talked at once. My brother reached for the crispiest rice. My grandfather complained that there was too much food while serving himself more. Grandmother ate last, watching us with a small, satisfied smile.

Years later, I moved away for university. One grey Sunday, surrounded by unpaid bills and a cold packet of noodles, my telephone rang.

“Come home,” Grandmother said. “I’ve forgotten how much saffron to use.”

She had forgotten nothing, of course. She simply stood beside me while I cooked, correcting me only when necessary. My rice stuck slightly. My onions were too dark. I had used far too much mint.

Still, when I lifted the lid, that familiar cloud of steam filled the kitchen.

Grandmother tasted a spoonful and considered it gravely.

“Not bad,” she said. “Next Sunday, you can make it again.”

That was when I understood why biryani was my favourite meal. It was not only the saffron rice, the tender chicken or the spices warming the back of my throat. It was the sound of chairs being pulled out, the promise that there would always be enough, and the knowledge that someone had saved me a place at the table.

content:
### The First King

Before there were kings, there was a valley with seven villages and one river, and every village believed the river belonged to it.

In dry summers they quarreled over its water. In wet springs they built walls against its floods. Each wall turned the river toward the next village, so that every act of safety became someone else’s ruin.

Then came a spring when the rain did not stop.

It drummed on the roofs for nineteen days. It filled the wells with mud and washed the seed from the fields. The river swallowed its banks, then the fish weirs, then the low road. On the twentieth night, the people of the lowest village fled uphill with their children on their backs and their cooking pots clutched to their chests.

The elders of the seven villages met beneath the standing stone on Council Hill.

“Break the western wall,” said one.

“And drown my orchards?” cried another.

“Then heighten the eastern wall.”

“So the water can come to us?”

They shouted until dawn. Each had a plan, and every plan required someone else to suffer.

At last a ferryman named Aren spoke. He was not an elder. He owned a boat, two goats, and a house small enough that he could touch opposite walls without straightening his arms. No one remembered inviting him.

“There is an old watercourse beyond the alder wood,” he said. “If we cut through the ridge, we can lead the flood into the empty marsh.”

The eldest chief laughed. “With what? Seven villages could dig until midsummer and not scratch that ridge.”

“Not if we spend another twenty days arguing.”

“And if your watercourse is a fairy tale?”

Aren looked toward the valley. Below them, something that had been a hayrick floated past.

“Then the river will kill us sooner instead of later.”

He told them what must be done. Every village would have to break down part of its own wall. Every village would have to send diggers. Food would be shared from a common store, and no one would keep watch over fields while another village worked.

The elders distrusted this, especially the last part.

“Who will decide how many diggers each village sends?” they asked.

“I will.”

“Who will say where the walls are broken?”

“I will.”

“And who will answer for it if you are wrong?”

Aren unwound the red mooring rope from his shoulder and laid it on the standing stone.

“I will.”

So they gave him authority until the flood went down. They did not do this because they loved him, or because they believed he had been chosen by heaven. They did it because they were frightened, and because he had offered them something none of the elders had offered: his own blame.

Aren took up the rope and went down the hill.

He did not stand on Council Hill pointing with a staff. He dug. When the people of the upper village refused to break their wall, he walked to his own village and struck the first blow against theirs. When the diggers’ food ran short, he gave away his goats. When the ridge proved thicker than he had promised, he confessed it before everyone and worked through the night beside them.

On the thirty-first day, the ridge broke.

The river entered the cutting with a sound like a mountain falling. It tore away spades, baskets, and three of the footbridges. Aren’s boat, which he had tied across the channel to carry workers, snapped its moorings and vanished. But the cutting held. The flood poured into the alder wood, then through the old watercourse, and spread at last across the empty marsh.

By morning, the river had begun to fall.

Aren returned to Council Hill, coated in mud to his eyebrows, and put the red rope back on the stone.

“It is done,” he said.

Then he went to find somewhere dry to sleep.

He might have been forgotten if matters had ended there. But after the flood came the reckoning.

One village had lost its orchards. Another had lost its wall. Two had lost most of their winter grain. Those whose fields had been spared did not wish to share their harvest with those whose fields had not. Old quarrels returned, and new ones sharpened themselves beside them.

So the villagers came to Aren.

They came first because he had been right about the river. They came again because he did not pretend to be right about everything else.

When two families claimed the same surviving cow, he walked the pasture and found her calf hidden beneath a cart. When the upper villages refused to rebuild the lower village’s houses, he asked whether they would prefer to rebuild their own after the next flood without help. When someone offered him the largest house in the valley as a reward, he gave it to the families who had been sleeping in the granary and built himself another small one beside the river.

At the end of that year, the elders returned the red rope to him.

“Only until matters are settled,” they said.

Matters were never entirely settled.

Each year Aren laid the rope upon the standing stone, and each year the people gave it back. Sometimes they argued for days before doing so. Once they chose a miller instead, but the miller wisely fled to his mill and refused to come out. In time, the rope became so worn that a smith made a thin circlet of iron from the seven digging blades used to open the ridge.

He set it upon Aren’s head during the harvest feast.

Aren immediately took it off.

“Why?” asked the smith, offended.

“Because it has no clasp.”

“It needs none.”

“It does if I am to give it back.”

So the smith opened a narrow gap in the iron. Only then would Aren wear it, and even then he hung it more often on a peg beside his door.

Years passed. The channel was widened. Common granaries were built. Children were born who could not remember the flood and found the whole story tiresome. When strangers entered the valley and asked who ruled it, the people pointed to Aren.

At first they simply called him by his name. Later, because names belong to persons and they needed a word for the work, they called him king.

Aren grew old beneath the iron circlet. His hair whitened, and his hands began to shake, but at the turning of every year he still carried the crown to Council Hill and placed it on the standing stone.

Once, a young man asked him, “Why should we obey you when the river is quiet?”

“You shouldn’t,” said Aren. “Obey the promises you made to one another. I only keep them where you can see them.”

When Aren died, they buried him above the old watercourse, where he could hear the river without being troubled by it. They set the iron crown on the standing stone. For three generations, whoever accepted the valley’s burdens wore it for a year and then put it back.

In the fourth generation, a man locked it in a treasury and declared that it belonged to his blood.

But that is another story, and a sadder one.

As for Aren, he did not become the first king when iron touched his brow. He became king on the morning when seven frightened villages placed their hands in his—and he understood, as almost no one afterward understood, that their hands had only been lent.
