content:
### The Moth

“You may look,” I said, “but don’t touch. People always touch the wrong part first. They want the edge, when the whole truth of a knife is in the handle.”

The young clerk lowered his hand.

I had agreed to answer three questions. He had wasted the first on my real name and the second on a number. I gave him neither. For the third, he nodded toward the object on the table.

“Of all the weapons you could have chosen,” he asked, “why that?”

It lay between us on a square of black linen, neither large nor impressive.

The blade was narrow as a willow leaf, its steel scoured to the grey of a winter sea. Held flat, it returned the lamplight as one thin white thread. Turned edge-on, it nearly vanished. There were no ripples in the metal, no gilded scrollwork, no jewels winking from the guard. At its base, almost rubbed away, was the maker’s stamp: a moth with open wings. One wing had disappeared entirely. The other remained, a crooked little line like a letter in a language no one bothered to teach.

The handle was pearwood, dark as strong tea. Years had polished it where the palm closed around it, but near the pommel the wood had dried and split. A pin of red copper held the split closed. The repair was ugly. I had always liked it for that.

Its sheath had once been oxblood leather. Now it was nearly black, soft at the mouth and stitched with waxed brown thread. When the blade slid free, it made no theatrical whisper—only a small, dry sound, like a tongue leaving the roof of a mouth.

“It isn’t beautiful,” the clerk said.

“No.”

He seemed pleased to have understood something.

“It isn’t ugly either,” I added. “It is exact.”

I picked it up. The weight settled behind my first finger, familiar as a ring. For a moment the lamplight moved along the steel and found the little moth.

“My mother was a bookbinder,” I said. “This was her paring knife. She used it on leather, thread, folded pages. She could open a book without breaking its spine. She could mend one so well that the owner would blame himself for ever thinking it damaged.”

The clerk glanced at his notebook. “So the choice was sentimental.”

“No. Sentiment is the story people tell when they run out of reasons.”

Outside, rain worried the windows. Somewhere below us, a door closed, and the clerk started at the sound. I pretended not to notice.

“I have used other weapons,” I said. “Each offers a kindness. Distance. Speed. Uncertainty. Some allow you to mistake a person for a problem of placement or timing. This allows nothing of the sort.”

I turned the knife once. The worn wood was warm from my hand.

“It keeps the work close. It keeps the face close. A weapon that makes its work easy also makes the work easy to repeat.”

“And that mattered to you?”

“It is the only thing that ever did.”

He looked disappointed. He had wanted secrets, perhaps: hidden compartments, an ingenious edge, some elegant cruelty he could carry away in ink. Instead I had given him reluctance.

I set the knife down.

“Last week,” I said, “I realized I could no longer remember whether the smoothness in the handle came from her hand or mine. For years I thought I was keeping her close. In fact, I was wearing her away.”

The clerk checked his watch. He thought I had not seen.

“Is that why you’re retiring?”

“Yes.”

“And your last contract?”

“Completed.”

His gaze flicked toward the sheathed blade, then to the locked door, then back to me. I almost laughed. Instead, I reached into my coat.

He stopped breathing.

I took out a book.

It was small and green, its binding faded at the corners. My mother had made it when I was a child. I had carried it for years without reading it; most of its pages were still joined at the folds.

I opened the cover and laid the book flat. Then I took up the knife.

The paper yielded with a sound unlike anything the clerk had been imagining. A soft tick. A curtain stirred by morning.

I freed the first two pages, then the next two. My mother’s old work came back through the handle: patience, pressure, the spine supported beneath the left palm. The little copper pin caught the light.

By the time the clerk remembered he had a fourth question, I had opened six pages and begun to read.

content:
# Timeline of Events

His father died on a Tuesday. Eli knew this because there was a form that said so.

The house smelled of machine oil and lemon polish. Clocks covered the walls of the workshop: carriage clocks, ship’s clocks, cheap plastic clocks with cartoon birds where the numbers should have been. His father had repaired them all, but none agreed on the time.

On the workbench, beneath a folded cloth, Eli found a black notebook.

**TIMELINE OF EVENTS — ELIAS WARD**  
**CORRECTED EDITION**

The first entry was written in his father’s narrow, careful hand.

**7 June 1991, 03:16 — Elias born.**  
*I had expected joy. Instead: terror. His hand closed around my finger. Event lasted approximately four seconds. Consequence: permanent.*

Eli sat down.

**14 September 1997, 08:42 — First day of school.**  
*E. asked whether clocks ever get tired. I said no. Incorrect.*

**22 November 2003, 19:10 — Mara died.**  
*E. sat beside me on the kitchen floor. I got up and wound the hall clock, though it did not need winding. At the time, I believed I was being useful.*

Eli remembered his mother’s funeral only in fragments: rain on the umbrella, the careful way his shoes pinched, his father polishing a clock that already shone.

He turned the page.

**8 May 2009, 21:36 — Argument.**  
*E. said I loved clocks more than people. I did not correct him. Clocks could be opened. Their faults could be found. This explanation seemed insufficient.*

**14 August 2010, 07:05 — E. left home.**  
*I said, “Then go.” Intended meaning: “Come back when you are ready.” Actual meaning, as heard: “Go.” Precision matters.*

There were entries after that, though Eli had not spoken to his father in years.

**3 October 2014 — E.’s photograph in the newspaper. He has his mother’s way of looking amused when he is trying not to be proud.**

**19 April 2017 — Granddaughter born. Name: Wren. Weight: 7 lb 2 oz. I have been informed this is average. She did not look average.**

Eli stopped reading.

He had never sent his father a photograph of Wren.

He looked toward the doorway, half expecting someone to confess to an elaborate cruelty. But the workshop was silent except for the clocks, ticking past and over one another.

He continued.

**2 June 2021 — E. called at 23:48. I did not answer. Reason given to myself: too late. Actual reason: I could not think of an opening sentence. Listened to message fourteen times. Message contained no request. Only: “It’s me. You don’t have to call back.”**

Eli shut the notebook.

For a while he listened to his own breathing. Then he opened it again.

The next entry was dated today.

**16 March, 18:04 — E. enters the workshop. He avoids the loose floorboard, although it was repaired when he was twelve.**

Eli looked at his watch: 18:11.

**18:11 — He notices the time.**

His skin prickled.

**18:19 — He says, “You could have just told me.” The workshop does not answer.**

At 18:19, Eli said, “You could have just told me.”

Nothing answered.

He almost laughed. Instead, he turned to the final page.

**18:26 — He considers putting the notebook away.**

**18:27 — He understands that an empty page is not the same as nothing.**

The rest was blank.

Eli took out his phone. Wren’s last message was from Sunday: a photograph of a cardboard solar system, each planet painted a ferocious, unlikely colour. Beneath it she had written, *Jupiter is the big one. You missed it.*

He had not replied because he had been ashamed, and shame had disguised itself as busyness.

At 18:31, he called her.

She answered on the fourth ring.

“Dad?”

“Hi,” he said. His voice sounded borrowed. “Tell me about Jupiter.”

There was a pause. Then Wren began to talk.

She told him Jupiter had taken three evenings because the paint kept turning brown. She told him Saturn’s ring had fallen off during assembly. She told him her teacher said space was mostly empty, but she thought that depended on what you counted as something.

Eli listened.

When she finally ran out of breath, he picked up his father’s pen.

**16 March, 18:42 — Called Wren. Did not promise to become a different person. Asked about the planets.**

Beneath his words, another line slowly appeared, the ink darkening letter by letter.

**Consequence: ongoing.**

Eli watched until the full stop formed. Then he turned the page and began a new timeline.

content:
The cursor is blinking at me like a small, impatient heart, so I write: *There is a blue bicycle at the bottom of the stairs.*

Then I hear a bell ring downstairs.

I go to look because apparently I am the sort of person who investigates impossible bicycles instead of finishing sentences, and there it is, leaning against the banister, blue as a robin’s egg, its tires wet though the pavement outside is dry. In the basket is a piece of paper folded once.

KEEP GOING, it says.

So I get on.

The street is empty. Not early-morning empty, not everyone-is-at-work empty, but emptied, as if the city has been rinsed out and set upside down to drain. No pigeons. No buses. No one behind the lit windows. I pedal past the bakery and think how good bread smells when it is first cut open, and immediately the air fills with steam and yeast. I think of a dog I had when I was nine, and something small and golden races beside me for half a block before becoming a scrap of sunlight.

This should frighten me, but the bicycle will not slow down, and besides, fear is difficult to maintain when the handlebars are streaming with silver ribbons.

I try to think only harmless thoughts. Tea. Socks. The laugh of the woman who sells flowers at the station. A cloud shaped like a whale. My brother.

No.

The street darkens.

I pedal faster, but he is already here in the way he always arrives: not his face, not at first, but the hospital corridor, the vending machine humming, the paper cup of coffee going cold between my hands. Eleven years collapses into one bad stripe of light on a tile floor. The bicycle turns left without me.

Now I am riding along the sea road near the house where we grew up. Gulls hang over the cliffs. The sky has that washed-out look it gets in old photographs. Ahead, our gate is open, and beyond it our mother’s yellow kitchen is glowing, though the house was sold and painted gray and stripped of every yellow thing long ago.

My brother is sitting on the front steps, peeling an orange.

He is seventeen. He will always be seventeen here, which seems unfair until he looks up and grins, and then it seems worse.

“You took your time,” he says.

“I didn’t know the way.”

“Neither did I.”

He holds out half the orange. I sit beside him. The sea booms below us, and somewhere inside the house a radio is playing the song he used to murder while washing dishes, all the high notes bent sideways.

“I’m sorry,” I say, because that is the sentence I have been carrying around like a stone in my shoe.

“For what?”

“For leaving. For not saying the right thing. For thinking there would be another day to say it in.”

He considers this seriously, the way he used to consider whether a sandwich needed more salt.

“You can’t revise me into staying,” he says.

“I know.”

“And you can’t keep writing the last page.”

“I know.”

“You clearly don’t.”

There it is—the annoyance, precise and familiar, and I start laughing. It shocks me more than the bicycle did. He laughs too, then steals back the orange half he gave me because I have forgotten to eat it.

Behind us, the bicycle bell rings.

“I have to go,” I say.

“Not yet. Tell me something else.”

“Like what?”

“Anything. Just not the hospital.”

So I tell him about the dog that raced beside me. I tell him the bakery still scorches the bottoms of its loaves, that our mother talks to her houseplants, that I once saw a cloud exactly shaped like a whale and had no one to call. I tell him he sang terribly. He tells me I peel oranges like a criminal.

When the bell rings again, I stand.

“What happens next?” I ask.

He looks toward the sea. “How should I know? You’re the one holding the pen.”

Then I am back at my desk. The cursor is still blinking. On the screen is the sentence about the bicycle, and beneath it, nothing.

My hands smell of oranges.

I could stop here. I could decide none of it happened. I could go downstairs and find the stairwell empty, make tea, become sensible.

Instead, I write: *My brother laughed.*

The words appear. They do not fix anything. They do not bring back the yellow kitchen or give us another summer. But somewhere far off, a bell answers, bright and small, and the next sentence begins to open like a road.
